source.quote: Greetings travelers, and welcome back to Goldbound, the challenge series where a rogue building locked is exploring Azeroth one zone at a time. And right now, we're making our way through the Eastern Kingdoms with the last episode unlocking the new zone of Dun Morogh, granting access to a brand new warband crafting alt, Golden Path, who is now equipped with leatherworking and blacksmithing. But so far, Dun Morogh is also home to pretty low farming rates. The trade goods like copper ore are currently clocking in around 900 to 1,200 gold per hour. So, we'll have to see if we can't bring those numbers up. But the downside from copper ore was smelting it into bars really wasn't profitable, and the usual shuffle of ores to bars and bars to handful of copper bolts was actually losing profit.

source.quote: And for reference, blue pigments are worth about 15 gold each right now, and this is relatively consistent across the other pigments that we can get here in Dun Morogh, such as Peacebloom to white pigment, which goes for 20 gold each. So before I farm the herbs and actually mill everything, I want to test which milling is the most profitable between classic milling and milling for housing pigments. And luckily, I do have a bit of a stockpile of some herbs, so I'm going to go ahead and mill up 100 Silverleaf, which have a base value of 200 gold, and see how much profit or loss I get from the housing pigments. And as far as the milling, there isn't much variety. 10 Silverleaf always mills down into one singular pigment, which means we're processing 20 gold worth of Silverleaf into 15 gold worth of pigment, which isn't very good. So our stack of 100 Silverleaf is now only worth 150 gold in pigments, which is a 50 gold loss. Unless the prices change wildly, the colored pigments just aren't worth it right now. However, with classic milling, the one we used back in Elwynn, the herbs of Peacebloom, Earthroot, and Silverleaf all mill into the same thing, Alabaster pigment. And luckily, milling this gives anywhere between two to four pigment per mill, and each mill only actually costs five of each herb, not 10. So the ratio is way better, and right now the price of Alabaster pigment is nine gold each. So our similar stack of 100 Silverleaf, when milled down to Alabaster pigments, goes from 200 gold to 594 gold. Even if the herbs are worth four gold each, like they can spike up to, that would be 400 gold of herbs to 594 gold of pigments, and it is definitely profitable. So, for now, the rates from 1 hour of farming, we pulled in a total of 164 Peacebloom, 232 Silverleaf, and 134 Earthroot. For a total raw trade good gold per hour, no processing yet, of 1,600. Not bad, and it beats out mining only. But, the reason I wanted to try herbalism wasn't necessarily for the raw goods, and since we unlearned mining and picked up inscription, let's get to milling. Of course, from our initial tests, we are just going straight to classic milling, and our stockpile of herbs, which is worth 1,600 gold, mills down into 349 Alabaster Pigments, which are worth 3,141 gold. A very nice profit, and this only took about 3 minutes to process, which puts the gold per hour for gathering into milling to over 3,000 gold per hour here. But, we can go a step further, because two Alabaster Pigments, which are worth nine gold each, 18 gold total, can be processed into a singular Moonglow Ink, which are worth over 20 gold. Now, that isn't a massive increase in profit, but nonetheless, it is an increase. So, once it's all said and done, we now have 75 Moonglow Inks from our total hours' worth of herbalism. And these, well, they're worth 3,669 gold. And the total processing time from herbs to inks was only 7 minutes. So, the perceived gold per hour, if we adjust for the total time of an hour and 7 minutes, is actually 3,313 gold per hour, which is notably more than double the value of the herbs alone, and it just required us some level one inscription skills to do. That is, indeed, very nice. But, as I was flying around here, I was running into quite a few rare spawns out in Dun Morogh. So, let's go take a look at them. Now, there aren't a ton of rares roaming around Dun Morogh, but they do spawn pretty fast. So, much like the Elwynn rares of Theros Lightfingers, Fed Fennel, and Mother Fang, these rares tend to spawn on a 15 to 30-minute cooldown. And one rare that I see quite a bit while farming herbs and spawning just to the west of Golebor Quarry in the dense herb areas is Bjarn, a rare polar bear. And since Bjarn is so findable, we're already at about an 11 kill count on him, and he doesn't drop any wild transmog with crazy values, but a few good items in the 1 to 2,000 gold range, with the best item being the black bear hide vest. So, whenever we're around him, whenever he pops up on the rare scanner, we're definitely going to tag him. Then up to the northwest in the troll camps of Shimmer Ridge, we have Great Father Arcticus, a rare spawn troll. And while most of his items are in the 30 to 40 gold range, there is one, the Frostmane Scepter, that has a market value closer to 60,000 gold and a listed drop rate of 2%. Although, like a lot of these old world drops in these old zones that were unavailable for some time and re-added in Cataclysm, that drop rate may be artificially low based on Wowhead reporting and tracking. But, we know it's not high, and uh we got it on the first kill. So, I'll count Goldilucky and get this one on the auction house to hopefully sell it while we're still in Dun Morogh, because with current token prices, a full ticket price sale on this is pretty much a quarter of a token. But, we will likely either have to wait a long time for it to sell or cut the price and sell it a little bit faster at wholesale prices.

source.quote: And for reference, blue pigments are worth about 15 gold each right now, and this is relatively consistent across the other pigments that we can get here in Dun Morogh, such as Peacebloom to white pigment, which goes for 20 gold each. So before I farm the herbs and actually mill everything, I want to test which milling is the most profitable between classic milling and milling for housing pigments. And luckily, I do have a bit of a stockpile of some herbs, so I'm going to go ahead and mill up 100 Silverleaf, which have a base value of 200 gold, and see how much profit or loss I get from the housing pigments. And as far as the milling, there isn't much variety. 10 Silverleaf always mills down into one singular pigment, which means we're processing 20 gold worth of Silverleaf into 15 gold worth of pigment, which isn't very good. So our stack of 100 Silverleaf is now only worth 150 gold in pigments, which is a 50 gold loss. Unless the prices change wildly, the colored pigments just aren't worth it right now. However, with classic milling, the one we used back in Elwynn, the herbs of Peacebloom, Earthroot, and Silverleaf all mill into the same thing, Alabaster pigment. And luckily, milling this gives anywhere between two to four pigment per mill, and each mill only actually costs five of each herb, not 10. So the ratio is way better, and right now the price of Alabaster pigment is nine gold each. So our similar stack of 100 Silverleaf, when milled down to Alabaster pigments, goes from 200 gold to 594 gold. Even if the herbs are worth four gold each, like they can spike up to, that would be 400 gold of herbs to 594 gold of pigments, and it is definitely profitable. So, for now, the rates from 1 hour of farming, we pulled in a total of 164 Peacebloom, 232 Silverleaf, and 134 Earthroot. For a total raw trade good gold per hour, no processing yet, of 1,600. Not bad, and it beats out mining only. But, the reason I wanted to try herbalism wasn't necessarily for the raw goods, and since we unlearned mining and picked up inscription, let's get to milling. Of course, from our initial tests, we are just going straight to classic milling, and our stockpile of herbs, which is worth 1,600 gold, mills down into 349 Alabaster Pigments, which are worth 3,141 gold. A very nice profit, and this only took about 3 minutes to process, which puts the gold per hour for gathering into milling to over 3,000 gold per hour here. But, we can go a step further, because two Alabaster Pigments, which are worth nine gold each, 18 gold total, can be processed into a singular Moonglow Ink, which are worth over 20 gold. Now, that isn't a massive increase in profit, but nonetheless, it is an increase. So, once it's all said and done, we now have 75 Moonglow Inks from our total hours' worth of herbalism. And these, well, they're worth 3,669 gold. And the total processing time from herbs to inks was only 7 minutes. So, the perceived gold per hour, if we adjust for the total time of an hour and 7 minutes, is actually 3,313 gold per hour, which is notably more than double the value of the herbs alone, and it just required us some level one inscription skills to do. That is, indeed, very nice. But, as I was flying around here, I was running into quite a few rare spawns out in Dun Morogh. So, let's go take a look at them. Now, there aren't a ton of rares roaming around Dun Morogh, but they do spawn pretty fast. So, much like the Elwynn rares of Theros Lightfingers, Fed Fennel, and Mother Fang, these rares tend to spawn on a 15 to 30-minute cooldown. And one rare that I see quite a bit while farming herbs and spawning just to the west of Golebor Quarry in the dense herb areas is Bjarn, a rare polar bear. And since Bjarn is so findable, we're already at about an 11 kill count on him, and he doesn't drop any wild transmog with crazy values, but a few good items in the 1 to 2,000 gold range, with the best item being the black bear hide vest. So, whenever we're around him, whenever he pops up on the rare scanner, we're definitely going to tag him. Then up to the northwest in the troll camps of Shimmer Ridge, we have Great Father Arcticus, a rare spawn troll. And while most of his items are in the 30 to 40 gold range, there is one, the Frostmane Scepter, that has a market value closer to 60,000 gold and a listed drop rate of 2%. Although, like a lot of these old world drops in these old zones that were unavailable for some time and re-added in Cataclysm, that drop rate may be artificially low based on Wowhead reporting and tracking. But, we know it's not high, and uh we got it on the first kill. So, I'll count Goldilucky and get this one on the auction house to hopefully sell it while we're still in Dun Morogh, because with current token prices, a full ticket price sale on this is pretty much a quarter of a token. But, we will likely either have to wait a long time for it to sell or cut the price and sell it a little bit faster at wholesale prices.

source.quote: He's also a bit unique because although he's mechanical, he's actually a tameable pet for hunters. So, any hunter gold bound challengers starting off in Dun Morogh, you might want to check this one out. Which leads us to the last rare of both Tinkertown and Dun Morogh. This is literally all of them in the whole zone. He's down to the south of Tinkertown in the toxic airfield. He's a leper gnome by the name of Gibblewilt, and he must be a foreman not just because he's barking orders, but because of his drops. The foreman pants and the foreman vest. Both of these items have a pretty solid value and are pretty rare, but not impossible. They're listed at a drop rate of 1.2% each, so it's definitely gettable. We haven't gotten it yet and we've tagged him a quite a few times, but we do fly right over this airfield during herb loops, so we're getting him quite a bit more. And between herb loops and the milling, no more getting runs and these rares, we're starting to have a pretty good setup for consistent gold and some rare transmog chances. So, if we get a little bit lucky on sales and drops, we might just be seeing a new zone spin sooner than we expected. Which gets me thinking, does the Dun Morogh unlock actually put any new zones onto the randomizer? Well, the only possible one I think would be Wetlands. The only issue is that the access to Wetlands from Dun Morogh, we have to go through one of the mountain passes, some of which lead directly into Loch Modan or possibly other off-limit zones. And after some research on my main path to avoid an accidental zone unlock here on Goldie, it seems like whichever way you go through the pass, you do either step directly into Loch Modan or the location of the pass at some point updates to Loch Modan and you discover it either way before you can actually get to the Wetlands. So, Wetlands will still be gated behind Loch Modan, which does mean the randomizer for the next unlock doesn't actually get a new zone, and we still have the options for Loch Modan, which of course is the gateway to the north, the Badlands, home to Uldaman, and then to the south, we're still rolling for Deadwind Pass, a meme zone, Blasted Lands of course, and then the Kalimdor unlock through the Barrens. So, there are some pretty interesting zones on the horizon for some spins. And one subzone here in Dun Morogh that we haven't paid much attention to, well, it's Coldridge Valley, the Northshire Abbey of the dwarves and the OG starting zone for gnomes. Now, for trade skills and trade goods, there isn't much to do here. It is a level one to six zone, so there's no herbs, no ores, and if you kill beasts, you can't even skin them here. But, there are some old items on the loot tables, items that were once available in Classic and Burning Crusade, which were then taken out of the game and unavailable for quite some time. This, of course, increased the price, but they have since been put back on the loot tables. And with avid collectors for collection logs and just transmog for whites becoming baseline, their value is real, and their drop rates, well, they're low. So, let's break this down. I have a shopping list for Goldie, which is basically just a list of all these items here that have some decent value and are rare, and I'm going to systematically farm them until I have them all. So, first up, let's head to the Frostmane trolls. And in the Frostmane hovel, the cave, we have the Frostmane blades, which luckily for us are actually on a hyper spawn here in this cave, killing them aimlessly and looting. So, let's update the boar target macro for heat-seeking Frostmanes and get to farming, because these guys, well, they have the Frostmane shortsword, and this white weapon has a market value of 16,000 gold and a drop rate from the blades at about 0.6%, which is low, but we can farm these guys unlimitedly and endlessly. So, we can stick around the cave and farm up a couple because to be honest, my plan isn't to get one of these and try to sell it for 16,000 gold full market price over the next couple of months. My plan is to get a few and sell them for wholesale prices because these items that have a high market value on TradeSkillMaster, most of them, if we post for 10 to 15% the posted market value, we will likely get purchased and bought out by auction house gold goblin snipers who are scanning for transmog or trade goods to flip. It's a bit of a win-win. They get a valuable long-term flip for a steal of a deal and Goldie gets an influx of cash sooner than later. Now, this isn't a sure fire way to do it. Generally speaking, a 10% price on transmog after a couple listings, it's probably getting bought out. Of course, once we're out of Dun Morogh and into other zones, if we have any of these left over, I'll just put them back into my regular market value transmog operations.
